extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and science journalists interested in retractions and misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating published research for signs warranting retraction—e.g., data fabrication, lack of IRB approval, unverifiable experiments, institutional validation, and use of statistical evidence. Focus is on determining which papers are tainted, which can be validated, and how journals act on institutional reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of data fabrication or falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers 'tainted by evidence of misconduct' and instances where the author 'acknowledged falsifying data' (e.g., 'manipulated the research period on purpose').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's admission of manipulating data is direct evidence; investigators look for signs such as impossible or inconsistent data. Such findings are grounds for retraction when substantiated. (Text: 'Dr. Fujii admitted that he manipulated the research period on purpose in these papers.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to obtain IRB approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies conducted without Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval are flagged as problematic ('Fujii also failed to obtain IRB approval').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of IRB approval, especially for human-subjects research, is a serious procedural and ethical breach and supports retraction when experiments purport to involve humans but no approval can be shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: False claims about study design (e.g., claiming RCT/double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that 'falsely claimed to be conducting randomized controlled double-blind trials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting study design (claiming randomized, controlled, or double-blind when not conducted) is a form of misconduct; verify protocol, randomization records, blinding procedures, and trial registration where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No supporting evidence that experiments were conducted
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where authors 'did not provide any evidence that he had conducted the experiments or that backed the authenticity of the data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators require raw data, lab notebooks, subject records, photos, or other documentation. Absence of any supporting material is strong evidence for retraction if authenticity cannot be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconclusive or unverifiable supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where 'investigators couldn’t find conclusive evidence of misconduct, but neither could they verify his results' and 'from a limited set of data ... it was not possible to confirm that the experiments were conducted exactly in the way described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial or limited datasets that fail to confirm methods/results create uncertainty; where verification is impossible, journals/institutions may still retract if integrity cannot be assured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evidence of fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions can be based on 'overwhelming statistical evidence of fabrication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical analyses (e.g., improbably regular distributions, duplicated numbers, anomalies inconsistent with sampling variability) as forensic indicators of possible data fabrication; such analyses have been used to justify retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional review and attestation of integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals requested institutions 'to attest to the integrity of published investigations' and used institutional responses to decide on retractions ('The response from each institution ... is available online').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional investigations and formal attestations are treated as authoritative input; journals act based on institutional reviews and may retract papers when institutions conclude misconduct or cannot validate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of some papers despite common authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Some coauthored papers were validated ('investigators concluded that five contained no evidence of misconduct' and an article by a coauthor 'remains part of the unimpeached medical literature').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each paper must be assessed individually; coauthorship does not automatically condemn or clear all associated papers—separate verification can identify unimpeached manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and categorizing suspected vs. validated papers for retraction totals
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining a final retraction total by subtracting validated papers from the original set of suspect papers ('...what’s left of the original 193 suspect papers minus the nine articles investigators ... were able to validate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep detailed records of suspect, validated, and retracted items; classification (clear fabrication, lack of IRB/no evidence, inconclusive) affects whether a paper is retracted and the final tally of retractions.
